newsitem.title: USA: Dive into latest Freddi fish mystery.
newsitem.headline: Dive into latest Freddi fish mystery.

text.p: Don't carp that its hard to find CD-ROM games for children. You can't pick a better computer adventure for kids ages 3 to 8 than "Freddi Fish 2: The Case of the Haunted Schoolhouse" (from Humongous Entertainment, Windows/Macintosh, $40).

This easy-to-play story of Freddi and her pal Luther, who try to uncover the true identity of a ghost that is terrorising their school of guppies, is first-rate in every way, from its top-flight animation to its delightful music.
The ghost is stealing the guppies' toys, such as Luther's Codfish Commando action figure.

Freddi, who has more sense than many real-life adults who are easily spooked by paranormal phenomenona, pursues the ghost to find out what's really going on. When she discovers that a nail has caught a piece of the ghost, she and Luther begin a scavenger hunt to build a trap for the creature.

As the adventure develops, players meet a host of interesting characters, including an underwater Elvis impersonator and a mumbling Squidfather, whose passing resemblance to a famous James Bond villian makes you wonder if his name shouldn't have been Blowfish.

The game has lots interesting places and objects to explore, a great sense of humour, and several stand-alone games to play, including a "Space Invaders"-style game with great sound effects and a drawing programme that's perfect for the 3-to-8 age group.
"Freddi" is cute without being sappy, and makes most other kids' products smell like week-old octopus. Dive in.
"Hunchback of Notre Dame: Topsy Turvy Games" (Windows, $40) wishes it could be as good.
This product from Disney Interactive features five routine games packaged in the milieu of the hit movie.

There's an old ball-and-paddle-style game involving a pigeon instead of a ball, a word game based on opposites, food-fight and balloon-popping games, and a bowling game where people are the pins, a goat is the ball and an aquatic monk named Bill who gets dunked in water after each strike looks suspiciously like a bearded Bill Clinton.

There's also a song, high-quality animation and plenty of banter from the three gargoyles, two of them voiced by Jason Alexander of "Seinfeld" and Charles Kimbrough of "Murphy Brown," who are reprising their movie roles.

The best joke in the game may be the "boss" key, the F11 key that makes the game instantly vanish if your boss passes by. Since "Hunchback" is designed for 7- to 15-year-olds, it probably should be called a "parent" key.

Look closely at the image that pops on the screen (an anatomical diagram of a pigeon), and you'll notice some odd names for the animal's claws (Gargoylia Grabiosum), neck (Bobbinus Neckius) and back (Pigeonus Saddleplaceous).

This is one of those games that sells based solely on the strength of the feature-length cartoon. Youngsters who have fallen in love with the gargoyle characters may find themselves enchanted by this CD-ROM, but others will be far less impressed. And parents might want to ask if this five-game package, at $8 per game, is worth the price.

Memorex didn't exactly pull out all the stops when it created "Gulliver's Voyage to Lilliput," an adaptation of the satire by Jonathan Swift, the witty dean of St. Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin, Ireland.

Watching this CD-ROM is like having a book on cassette tape and being able to follow along with a real book. The animation is as crude as you can get, consisting mostly of cutout figures that drift across the screen.
"Gulliver" also offers a game that lets you reconstruct a jumbled picture. However, with only four pictures to put together, it's only entertaining for about five minutes.
The real attraction here is the story by Swift, whose tale of a ship's surgeon captured by a race of people who are less than 6 inches tall was intended to make fun of people in high office.

"Gulliver's Travels" was originally published in 1726 under the authorship of Lemuel Gulliver, an attempt by Swift to give the story a ring of truth. The book, before it was adapted as a children's tale, had three other parts. Gilliver's second voyage was to a land of giants, the third to the flying island of Laputa and the last to a land of wise, talking horses.

None of these other tales and none of the background about Swift is mentioned on this CD-ROM. The product also lacks a decent instruction book and you have to know how to switch your computer's video display from the standard 256 colours to 64,000 colours, which isn't always easy.

Ultimately, what you get from "Gulliver's Voyage to Lilliput" is a CD-ROM that lets the computer read a 96-page book to you in about an hour. Yet, because the price is only about $15, consumers may find its drawbacks easy to overlook. Distributed by N-TK Inc., it's available for personal computers with Windows.
(Gene Emery is a columnist who covers science and technology. His Internet address is gene.emery(at)prodigy.com. Opinions in the column are his alone.)
